extraction.paper_title: Fast Thermal Goodness Evaluation of a 3D-IC Floorplan

scenario.figure_or_table: Figure 10 (FP1 vs FP2 example, n100 GSRC benchmark, 4-layer 3D floorplans)
scenario.description: Published comparison of two sample 4-layer 3D floorplans (FP1: area 0.319 mm2, peak temperature 564 K; FP2: area 0.326 mm2, peak temperature 567 K) of the GSRC n100 benchmark, where the power-based thermal goodness value (TGV) is compared against HotSpot peak temperature. Module-level coordinates and powers are not published; module power densities were randomly assigned from 1e5-1e7 W/m2.
scenario.architecture: 4-layer TSV-based 3D IC stack with heat sink on top, 45 nm technology node assumed, GSRC n100 floorplans generated by a non-deterministic evolutionary 3D floorplanner that co-places TSVs and modules
scenario.workload: Random module power densities (1e5 to 1e7 W/m2) assigned to GSRC benchmark modules; no activity or workload trace
scenario.operating_point: Steady-state HotSpot peak temperature (FP1 564 K, FP2 567 K); TGV evaluated on a 64x64x4 grid

original_setup.solver: HotSpot (steady-state, default parameters) peak-temperature simulation as the reference; the proposed power-based Thermal Goodness Value (TGV) is evaluated on an nxnxl grid (64x64x4 for the selected scenario). Heat sink is on top of the 4-layer stack (pdf pages 2, 4).
original_setup.optimizer: Non-deterministic evolutionary 3D floorplanner that co-places TSVs and modules. It is built on the Nain and Chrzanowska-Jeske 3D floorplanner, which extends ELF-SP. It generated the floorplans that are only evaluated, not thermally optimized, in this paper (pdf pages 2, 4).
original_setup.controller: None. There is no dynamic thermal controller or transient control. The study screens static floorplans.
original_setup.benchmark: GSRC n100 benchmark, 4-layer 3D floorplans FP1 (area 0.319 mm2, peak temperature 564 K) and FP2 (area 0.326 mm2, peak temperature 567 K), pdf page 6, Figure 10. Module power densities were randomly assigned from 1e5-1e7 W/m2 at an assumed 45 nm node (pdf page 2).

thermal_observable.location: HotSpot peak temperature of the 4-layer 3D floorplan FP1 of the n100 benchmark. Layer 0 is the farthest from the heat sink and is the hottest layer.
thermal_observable.aggregation: Peak (maximum) temperature over the 3D stack from steady-state HotSpot. FP2 is 567 K. Values are read from the text of the Figure 10 discussion.

physical_mismatches.reason: The scenario is a 4-layer TSV-based 3D IC with vertical heat conduction through the active Si, BEOL SiO2 and TIM layers. A 2D, single-layer Studio model cannot represent inter-layer heat transfer, TSV islands (treated as zero-power modules), or layer 0 being farthest from the heat sink.

The original thermal metric is a power-based TGV (a sum of 2x2 sub-grid power densities adjusted for neighbor cells) alongside HotSpot peak temperature. It is not a finite-difference temperature solution, so the Studio solver cannot reproduce the paper's TGV or its HotSpot-vs-TGV correlation and success-rate analysis.

The paper's optimizer is an evolutionary 3D floorplanner generating many floorplans, and its goal is ranking floorplan pairs, not optimizing a single design. The selected FP1/FP2 comparison involves no controller, transient behaviour or reliability analysis, so any Studio optimizer or controller is not part of the original experiment.

Module coordinates, dimensions and powers for FP1/FP2 are not published. Power densities were randomly assigned (1e5-1e7 W/m2) and no per-module watts exist, so a faithful geometry and power input cannot be built. Cooling is described only as a heat sink on top, with no HotSpot package parameters beyond 'default'.

studio_assumptions: No complete experiment is reproducible. The floorplan must stay empty (no paper-derived blocks, coordinates or power_rows). Total chip power is not split among modules.
Any bundled Studio package, material and cooling assumptions are Studio-side. They are not taken from the paper and are not equivalent to the HotSpot default 3D stack with a top-mounted heat sink.

If a runner builds a separate illustrative 2D placement and one-row power trace from dimensions and powers, its generated coordinates are distinct from paper facts. Its temperatures must not be compared numerically to 564 K or 567 K.
The paper's only published numeric facts for this scenario are the FP1/FP2 areas and HotSpot peak temperatures (pdf page 6), and no complete set of geometry, power and boundary data accompanies them.

methods.note: The TGV method (grid translation, neighbor-cell adjustment, 2x2 sub-grid sums), the HotSpot reference, the evolutionary 3D floorplanner lineage, the top-mounted heat sink and the pair-comparison protocol are supported by text on pages 2-6. Two caveats. First, the pairing of 'steady-state HotSpot default parameters' with the Figure 10 temperatures is inferred from the page 4 runtime discussion. Second, the extraction's own mismatch list correctly says the 3D, TGV and ranking-study features cannot be mapped to a 2D steady solver.

code.note: The paper says the floorplanner and TGV were written in C++ (page 4) but gives no repository, availability statement or link. The extraction's 'no links' conclusion rests on extracted PDF text only. No assets were supplied, so no code was inspected.

parameters.note: The text confirms 564 K, 567 K, 0.319 mm2, 0.326 mm2, 1e5-1e7 W/m2, 45 nm, four layers and the unit conversions (mm2 to m2 x1e-6; nm to m x1e-9). The decisive inputs are absent: per-module power densities and watts, layer thicknesses, TIM, TSV island parameters, and ambient or sink parameters. The 64x64x4 grid for the Figure 10 pair is not stated in the paper for that figure. The meaning of 'area' (footprint versus total across layers) is not stated.

config.note: HotSpot is described only as 'default parameters' (page 4, in the runtime comparison). There is no HotSpot configuration file, package or heat-sink convection setting, and no ambient temperature. The extraction's 'custom_2d_steady' kind with an empty floorplan does not match a faithful configuration of this 3D scenario.

data.note: The only data are two text-stated peak temperatures and two areas. No module coordinates, per-module power, or TGV values for FP1/FP2 were provided. Figure 10 was never supplied as an image or asset, so no figure value was visually verified. Same-scenario power for every floorplan block does not exist, and correctly no blocks were built.

findings.reason: The extraction asserts that TGV was evaluated on a 64x64x4 grid 'for the selected scenario'. The paper never states the grid used for the Figure 10 FP1/FP2 comparison. 64x64x4 is only the headline grid in the abstract and Table 1. The extraction's own uncertainty field concedes this, yet the scenario and setup present it as fact.

'Steady-state' and 'default parameters' are tied to the Figure 10 peak temperatures. Page 4 uses these phrases only for the runtime comparison. Applying them to the FP1/FP2 temperatures is an inference.

assessment.summary: 2D screening label: not_2d_applicable. Studio did not run (simulation status skipped; simulation_allowed false) because the custom experiment has no blocks and no power_w object, so input validity failed. The deterministic gate sets comparison_valid to false and input_gate_pass and scientific_gate_pass to false. The scenario is the Figure 10 FP1 vs FP2 comparison of 4-layer 3D floorplans of the GSRC n100 benchmark. The only published numbers are FP1 area 0.319 mm2 with HotSpot peak 564 K, FP2 area 0.326 mm2 with peak 567 K, a random power-density range of 1e5-1e7 W/m2, and a 45 nm node assumption. The experiment kind is custom_2d_steady, so it is a steady run with no transient trace. It is not a bundled EV6/GCC adapted demonstration, and no pinned Ascend910 or ATPlace sizes and powers were supplied. No illustrative input.flp or one-row input.ptrace was generated, so there is no source commit or generated-placement assumption to report. No Studio temperature exists. The 564 K and 567 K values are HotSpot steady-state peak temperatures over a 4-layer stack with a top heat sink, and they cannot be matched numerically to any 2D result. Any future 2D run would differ in location (3D stack peak, layer 0 hottest, vs single layer), aggregation, vertical conduction, TSV treatment, and package and boundary assumptions. At most one could discuss qualitative sensitivity, for example that a slightly larger area FP2 had a slightly higher peak than FP1. This is not exact replication, and no thermal conclusion is drawn from Studio for this paper.
